Outline

Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics ​

Rates and Curves ​

Spot Rate ​

NOTE

All rates are annualized unless specified otherwise.

  • A spot rate is the rate, observed today, for a single payment at a future date. It is the yield on a zero-coupon bond of that maturity, so it is also called the zero rate. Spot rates are usually taken from default-free (government) bonds.
  • sn is the spot rate for maturity n years.
  • The spot curve (zero curve) plots the spot rates sn against maturity n.
  • Few zero-coupon bonds trade at long maturities, so long-term spot rates are usually inferred by bootstrapping from the prices of coupon bonds: solve for s1 from the one-year bond, then use it to solve for s2 from the two-year bond, and so on.
  • The spot curve changes over time: today's curve is a snapshot, and tomorrow's will differ.

Discount factor. P(j) is the value today of 1 paid in year j:

P(j)=1(1+sj)j

It is fundamentally a transform of the spot rate that turns discounting into a multiplication: PV=FV×P(j). Discount factors are below 1 and fall as maturity lengthens. In the chart, s5=3.30% gives P(5)=1/1.0335=0.8502.

Forward Rate ​

Forward Rate and Forward Curve ​

A forward rate is the interest rate, agreed today, for a loan that starts at a future date and runs for a set period. It locks in today the rate for borrowing or lending between two future dates.

  • f(j,k) is the forward rate for a loan starting in year j and running for k years, so it ends in year j+k.
  • Similarly, the forward discount factor F(j,k) is the value at year j of 1 paid in year j+k:
F(j,k)=1(1+f(j,k))k

The forward curve in Level II is the term structure of forward rates: forward rates against their tenor k, all with the same initiation date j. The spot curve is the forward curve with j=0.

NOTE

This definition is different from Level I, which plots a series of forward rates that each have the same tenor (e.g., one-year forwards f(1,1),f(2,1),f(3,1),…) against the year they start or end.

Each initiation date gives its own forward curve:

In practice, the bond market usually draws them against calendar years: each curve starts at its initiation year, and each point sits at the year its loan ends.

Forward Rate Models ​

Forward rates follow from spot rates (covered in Level I). Investing for two years at s2 must give the same result as investing for one year at s1 and then rolling into the one-year forward rate f(1,1):

(1+s2)2=(1+s1)(1+f(1,1))

In general:

(1+sj+k)j+k=(1+sj)j(1+f(j,k))k

The equality is guaranteed by arbitrage: if the forward rate were higher, investors would lend forward and borrow spot, and vice versa, until the two routes paid the same.

Example. With s1=2.00%, s2=2.40% and s3=2.75% (the curve in the charts):

f(1,1)=1.02421.02−1=1.0485761.02−1=2.80%f(1,2)=(1.027531.02)1/2−1=(1.0847901.02)1/2−1=3.13%

NOTE

A shortcut for calculation. When x→0, (1+x)a≃1+ax. If (1+r1)a=(1+r2)b(1+r3)c with a=b+c, then

1+ar1≃(1+br2)(1+cr3)=1+br2+cr3+bcr2r3≃1+br2+cr3

because the product of two small rates is negligible. So ar1≃br2+cr3: the longer rate is roughly the time-weighted average of the shorter ones. In the example, f(1,1)≃2×2.40%−2.00%=2.80% and f(1,2)≃(3×2.75%−2.00%)/2=3.125%, very close to the exact answers.

Given the spot rates, every forward rate, and therefore every forward curve, can be derived. In practice, long-term spot rates are much less accurate, because they are inferred from few, less liquid bonds, so long-dated forwards inherit that error.

The same relationship holds for discount factors, where it is simply multiplication:

P(j+k)=P(j)F(j,k)F(j,k)=P(j+k)P(j)

Relationship between Curves ​

When the spot curve is increasing, the forward curves lie above it. When it is decreasing, they lie below it.

Why. Apply the shortcut to the forward rate model:

(j+k)sj+k≃jsj+kf(j,k)f(j,k)≃sj+k+jk(sj+k−sj)

The long spot rate sj+k is a weighted average of sj and f(j,k), so the forward rate must lie on the far side of it from sj:

  • Increasing spot curve: sj+k>sj, so f(j,k)>sj+k≥sk. The forward curve is above the spot curve.
  • Decreasing spot curve: sj+k<sj, so f(j,k)<sj+k≤sk. The forward curve is below the spot curve.

For example, f(2,3)≃3.30%+23(3.30%−2.40%)=3.90%, above s5=3.30%, and the exact value is also 3.90%.

Whether the forward curve itself rises or falls depends on the convexity of the spot curve, not just on its slope. With continuous compounding, the spot rate is the average of the instantaneous forward rates, ts(t)=∫0tf(u)du. Differentiating:

f(t)=s(t)+ts′(t)f′(t)=2s′(t)+ts″(t)
  • f−s=ts′: the forward is above the spot curve exactly when the spot curve is rising, as above.
  • Linear spot curve (s″=0): f′=2s′, so the forward curve slopes the same way, twice as steeply.
  • Concave rising spot curve (s″<0): the forward curve rises at first, but peaks and turns down where ts″(t)=−2s′(t), while still staying above the spot curve.
  • Convex rising spot curve (s″>0): the forward curve rises even faster.

The discrete version is the same idea: the one-year forward is f(n,1)≃sn+1+n(sn+1−sn), so it falls once the spot curve's increments shrink fast enough.

Shapes of the yield curve. In developed markets, yield curves are usually increasing and concave: yields rise with maturity, but by less and less (a diminishing marginal yield). A rough economic explanation (covered in detail later in Fixed Income):

  • Nominal yields include a premium for expected inflation, which is associated with relatively strong economic growth.
  • Investors demand a risk premium for holding longer bonds, which adds to the positive slope.

Other shapes:

  • An inverted (downward-sloping) curve is uncommon. It may reflect market expectations of declining future inflation and policy rates, for example ahead of a recession. The real-world causes are more complex and often policy-related; see the US 10-year minus 3-month spread on FRED (T10Y3M).
  • A flat curve typically occurs as a brief transition between an upward-sloping and an inverted curve.
  • A humped curve, with intermediate maturities yielding the most, is rare.

Par Rate ​

The par rate for maturity n is the coupon rate that makes an n-year bond priced at par, when its cash flows are discounted at the spot rates. Writing parn for that coupon rate, with a par value of 1:

parn1+s1+parn(1+s2)2+⋯+1+parn(1+sn)n=1

In discount factors, parn∑i=1nP(i)+P(n)=1, so

parn=1−P(n)∑i=1nP(i)

When a bond is priced at par, its YTM = coupon rate = par rate.

The par curve plots the par rates against maturity n. A par bond's yield is an average of the spot rates up to its maturity, so when the spot curve rises, the par curve sits slightly below it (and above it when the spot curve falls).

Example. With s1=2.00% and s2=2.40%: P(1)=0.98039 and P(2)=0.95367, so

par2=1−0.953670.98039+0.95367=2.395%

Bootstrapping. Spot rates can be obtained from the par curve by bootstrapping (see Spot Rate), one maturity at a time:

  • par1=s1: a one-year par bond has a single cash flow.
  • Each later spot rate is inferred from parn and the spot rates already found. For n=2:
0.023951.02+1.02395(1+s2)2=1

which gives s2=2.40%.

YTM ​

The yield to maturity (YTM) is the single discount rate that sets the present value of a bond's cash flows equal to its price:

P=∑t=1NCFt(1+y)t
  • It is the discount rate used in ordinary bond calculations.
  • It can be viewed as a kind of average of the spot rates, weighted by the bond's cash flows.
  • If the spot curve is flat, the YTM equals the spot rate.

For example, a 3-year 5% annual-coupon government bond, discounted at s1=2.00%, s2=2.40% and s3=2.75%, is priced at 106.46. Its YTM is 2.73%: between s1 and s3, and close to s3, because most of the cash flow comes in year 3.

The YTM is the expected return only under three assumptions:

  • All coupon and principal payments are made in full and on time.
  • The bond is held until maturity.
  • All cash flows are reinvested at the YTM.

The expected return is the ex-ante return an investor expects to earn; the realized return is the return actually earned. The YTM is often a poor estimate of either, because in real life:

  • Interest rates are volatile, so reinvestment rates and selling prices change.
  • When the yield curve is steeply sloped, coupons cannot all be reinvested at the YTM.
  • There is a risk of default.
  • The bond may have embedded options, which change its cash flows.

Swap Rate ​

NOTE

Swaps are covered mostly in Derivatives: see Interest Rate Swap, including how the swap rate is priced and a worked example.

The swap rate is the interest rate of the fixed-rate leg of an interest rate swap. In a plain vanilla swap, one side pays the fixed swap rate and the other pays a floating market reference rate (MRR, such as SOFR; formerly LIBOR), on the same notional.

Pricing. At initiation the swap has zero value, so PV(fixed leg)=PV(floating leg). Add a hypothetical exchange of the notional at the end (it cancels out): the two legs become a fixed-rate bond and a floating-rate bond, and Vswap=Vfixed−Vfloat=0.

  • A floating-rate bond's coupon resets to the market rate, the same rate used to discount it, so it is priced at par on each reset date: Vfloat=par.
  • Therefore Vfixed=par too. The swap rate is the coupon that prices a fixed-rate bond at par: the par rate on the swap curve.
Swap rateN=1−P(N)∑i=1NP(i)

where the discount factors come from the MRR (swap) curve.

The yield curve of swap rates is the swap rate curve (swap curve). It is simply an application of the par curve to swaps; there is no fundamental difference.

Why investors often prefer the swap curve to the government spot curve as a benchmark:

  • The swap market offers more maturities.
  • The swap market is highly liquid, unlike many bond markets, and swaps are one of the most efficient ways to hedge interest rate risk.
  • Swap rates reflect the credit risk of commercial banks, which use swaps the most, rather than of the government, so they are closer to private-sector borrowing costs.
  • The swap market is not regulated by any government (swaps trade OTC, while government bond markets are shaped by each government), so swap rates are more comparable across countries.

Spread ​

NOTE

Less important than the previous parts.

A yield spread is the difference between a bond's yield and a benchmark yield: Spread=yA−yB. The main types:

SpreadDefinition
G-spread (nominal)Bond yield − government bond yield of the same maturity
I-spread (nominal)Bond yield − swap rate of the same maturity
Z-spreadConstant spread over the government spot curve that prices the bond
OAS (option-adjusted spread)Z-spread adjusted for embedded options (covered later)

Swap spread (calculation required):

Swap spreadN=Swap rateN−ygov,N

where ygov,N is the yield on the on-the-run government bond of the same maturity N.

It reflects mainly the extra credit risk of the banks behind swap rates over the government, together with differences in liquidity between the two markets.

I-spread:

I-spreadN=ybond,N−Swap rateN

The I-spread reflects the bond's credit and liquidity risk relative to swaps: swaps carry bank credit risk and are more liquid than most corporate bonds. "I" stands for interpolated, because the swap rate for the bond's exact maturity is often interpolated between quoted maturities.

The spreads add up: G-spread=Swap spread+I-spread, i.e., government → swap → corporate.

Example (I-spread). A 6-year corporate bond yields 4.80%. Swap rates are 3.60% for 5 years and 3.90% for 7 years; government bonds yield 3.20% for 5 years and 3.40% for 7 years.

  • Interpolated 6-year swap rate =3.60%+6−57−5(3.90%−3.60%)=3.75%
  • I-spread =4.80%−3.75%=1.05%, or 105 bps
  • Interpolated 6-year government yield =3.30%, so the G-spread is 150 bps and the swap spread 3.75%−3.30%=45 bps: 45+105=150

TED spread = 3-month MRR (LIBOR) − 3-month T-bill rate.

  • It reflects credit risk in the general economy: an increase in the TED spread signals that lenders (banks) believe the risk of default is increasing.
  • It can be thought of as a measure of counterparty risk between banks.
  • Because it compares bank borrowing with government borrowing, it is a widely used gauge of risk in the banking system.

MRR–OIS spread (LIBOR–OIS) = MRR − OIS rate.

The OIS rate is the fixed rate of an overnight indexed swap, whose floating leg is the geometric average of an overnight rate over every day of the payment period:

1+rfloat⋅D360=∏i=1D(1+ri⋅1360)

The overnight rate carries almost no credit risk, so the spread measures the credit and liquidity risk of bank lending over the term; it widened sharply in the 2008 crisis.

NOTE

LIBOR has been phased out (2021–2023) and replaced by rates such as SOFR. The curriculum's spreads still work with any MRR.

Z-spread. The zero-volatility spread is the constant spread Z that, added to every government spot rate, discounts a risky bond's cash flows to its price:

P=∑t=1NCFt(1+st+Z)t

The parallel shift of the spot curve is an assumption: in reality, credit spreads usually differ by maturity.

Example. A 3-year 5% annual-coupon corporate bond is priced at 102.14, with spot rates of 2.00%, 2.40% and 2.75%. Try Z=1.50%:

51.035+51.0392+1051.04253=4.831+4.632+92.675=102.14

So the Z-spread is 150 bps. If the bond has an embedded option, use the OAS instead, covered later.

Traditional Term Structure Theories ​

IMPORTANT

This part is important.

These theories explain the economic factors that determine the shape of the yield curve. Write E[sk(j)] for today's expectation of the k-year spot rate in year j.

Pure Expectations Theory ​

The forward rate is an unbiased predictor of the future spot rate:

f(j,k)=E[sk(j)]

For example, f(1,1)=E[s1(1)]: the one-year forward rate starting in one year equals the one-year spot rate expected in one year.

So the shape of the curve shows only expected future rates:

  • Upward-sloping spot curve: short rates are expected to rise
  • Flat: expected to stay the same
  • Downward-sloping: expected to fall

The theory assumes investors are risk neutral. In real life, investors are risk averse. An equivalent interpretation is that bonds of any maturity are perfect substitutes: every strategy over the same horizon (a 2-year bond, or two 1-year bonds rolled over, or a 10-year bond sold after 2 years) has the same expected return.

Local Expectations Theory ​

This theory relaxes the risk-neutral assumption: it requires risk neutrality only over short holding periods. Over a short period, every default-free bond, whatever its maturity, is expected to earn the risk-free short rate. Over longer periods, risk premiums are allowed. The other conclusions are the same as under the pure expectations theory.

NOTE

In practice the theory does not hold either: over short periods, long-term bonds tend to earn more than short-term bonds, which suggests a premium for holding them.

Liquidity Preference Theory ​

Investors demand a liquidity premium to compensate for the added risk of longer-maturity bonds. The theory adds this premium to the pure expectations theory:

f(j,k)=E[sk(j)]+LP(j,k),LP>0

The liquidity premium is positive and increases with maturity. The conclusions are those of the pure expectations theory, adjusted for the premium:

  • Upward-sloping curve: uncertain. Rates may be expected to rise, stay flat, or even fall slightly, if the premium is large enough.
  • Flat curve: rates are expected to fall slightly, because the positive premium must be offset by a lower expected rate.
  • Downward-sloping curve: rates are expected to fall significantly.

Segmented Market Theory ​

Yields in each maturity segment are set by the supply and demand for funds in that segment, independently of the yields in other segments.

  • It is consistent with a world of asset–liability management constraints (e.g., regulation, or different investment policy statements) that tie investors to certain maturities.
  • Yields are not a reflection of expected spot rates or liquidity premiums.

Preferred Habitat Theory ​

Investors and borrowers prefer certain maturities (their habitats), but will deviate from them if the premium is high enough.

  • The premium is not directly related to maturity: it depends on supply and demand in each segment, so the theory can explain any curve shape, including a humped one.
  • Investors will accept additional risk for additional return.

NOTE

The key difference from the segmented market theory: there, markets cannot influence each other; here, a high enough premium draws investors across segments.

TheoryForward rateAn upward-sloping curve means
Pure expectations=E[future spot]Rates expected to rise
Local expectationsSame, over short horizonsRates expected to rise
Liquidity preference=E[future spot]+LP, LP rising with maturityUncertain
Segmented marketsNot related to expectationsSupply and demand in each segment
Preferred habitat=E[future spot]+ premium, not tied to maturityDepends on supply and demand

Yield Curve Factor Models ​

Yield Curve Movement ​

Yield curve movements can be decomposed into three factors:

  • Level, a parallel shift: ΔXL
  • Steepness, a change in the slope: ΔXS
  • Curvature, a change in the bend: ΔXC

Each factor has a fixed shape across maturities, and a move scales it. The change in the yield at maturity t is approximately

Δy(t)≈ΔXL+ΔXSσ(t)+ΔXCκ(t)

where σ(t) rises with maturity (short end down, long end up) and κ(t) is U-shaped (ends up, middle down).

The decomposition is useful because the first factor, or the first two, usually explain most of a curve move: the level factor explains most of the variation in yields (it has the highest R2), and steepness and curvature most of the rest. For a parallel shift, effective duration alone is enough, which is much easier than key rate durations.

Review: Duration and Convexity (Level I) ​

  • Macaulay duration is the weighted-average time to the bond's cash flows, weighted by their present values:
MacDur=∑t=1Nt⋅PV(CFt)P
  • Modified duration converts it into a price sensitivity to the bond's own yield, with r the yield per period:
ModDur=MacDur1+rΔPP≈−ModDur⋅Δy
  • Approximate modified duration, from prices at yields ±Δy:
ApproxModDur=PV−−PV+2⋅Δy⋅PV0
  • Effective duration uses the same formula, but shifts the benchmark yield curve by ±ΔCurve and reprices the bond with a model. It is the measure for bonds with embedded options, whose cash flows change with rates:
EffDur=PV−−PV+2⋅ΔCurve⋅PV0
  • Money (dollar) duration =ModDur×P, the change in value in currency units; the price value of a basis point is PVBP=PV−−PV+2 for a 1 bp shift.
  • Convexity captures the curvature of the price–yield relationship:
ApproxCon=PV−+PV+−2PV0(Δy)2⋅PV0
  • Together:
ΔPP≈−ModDur⋅Δy+12Convexity⋅(Δy)2

Exact modified duration and convexity. Both are rates of change of the price, relative to the price:

ModDur=−1P⋅dPdyConvexity=1P⋅d2Pdy2

The approximate formulas above are numerical (central-difference) estimates of these derivatives: PV−−PV+2Δy estimates −dPdy, and PV−+PV+−2PV0(Δy)2 estimates d2Pdy2.

For a zero-coupon bond they have a closed form, because there is only one cash flow. With face value F, maturity n and yield y per period:

P=F(1+y)−n

Each derivative brings down the exponent and adds one power of (1+y) to the denominator:

dPdy=−nF(1+y)−(n+1)d2Pdy2=n(n+1)F(1+y)−(n+2)

Dividing by the price cancels the (1+y)−n in it, leaving only the powers added by differentiating, one for duration and two for convexity:

ModDur=nF(1+y)−(n+1)F(1+y)−n=n1+yConvexity=n(n+1)F(1+y)−(n+2)F(1+y)−n=n(n+1)(1+y)2

So the denominator is (1+y)2 whatever the maturity: the maturity appears only in n(n+1). The Macaulay duration of a zero is its maturity n, consistent with ModDur=MacDur/(1+y).

For a 5-year zero at 4% (price 82.193 per 100), the approximate formulas converge to the exact values, 5/1.04=4.808 and 30/1.042=27.737, as Δy shrinks:

ΔyPV−PV+ModDurConvexity
1%86.26178.3534.81127.749
0.1%82.58981.7994.80827.737
0.01%82.23282.1534.80827.737
Exact4.80827.737

NOTE

In the exam, use the approximate formulas with PV− and PV+. The closed form is a shortcut for zero-coupon bonds only; a coupon bond has several cash flows, so its exact convexity is a sum over them, 1P∑tt(t+1)CFt(1+y)t+2.

Example. A 5-year zero-coupon bond yields 4%. From the closed forms above, its Macaulay duration is 5, ModDur=5/1.04=4.808 and its convexity is 30/1.042=27.74. If the yield rises by 1%:

ΔPP≈−4.808×0.01+12×27.74×0.012=−4.669%

The exact change is (1.04/1.05)5−1=−4.672%.

NOTE

All the Level I conclusions, including the ΔP/P formula, assume a parallel shift of a flat yield curve. In Level II we also study non-parallel movements.

Key rate duration measures a bond's sensitivity to a small change in the benchmark yield curve at one specific maturity (a key rate), holding the other key rates constant.

Key Rate Duration ​

IMPORTANT

The most important part of M1.

KeyRateDurk=−1PV⋅ΔPVΔrk

where Δrk is a shift of the k-th key rate of the benchmark curve only.

Key rate duration is a curve duration, not a yield duration.

  • A yield duration (Macaulay, modified, approximate modified) measures the sensitivity of the price to the bond's own YTM. It treats the bond as if all its cash flows were discounted at that one yield, so it cannot say what happens when different parts of the curve move differently.
  • A curve duration (effective duration, key rate duration) measures the sensitivity to a shift in the benchmark yield curve, repricing every cash flow at its own rate. Effective duration shifts the whole curve; a key rate duration shifts one point of it.
  • For an option-free bond and a flat curve, the two give almost the same number. They differ when the curve is not flat, when it moves in a non-parallel way, or when the bond has embedded options.

Example. A portfolio of two zero-coupon bonds, worth 100 in total: bond 1 is worth 40 and matures in 3 years; bond 2 is worth 60 and matures in 5 years. For simplicity take each bond's duration as its maturity (modified duration would be slightly lower, n/(1+y)).

  • 3-year rate up 1%, all other rates unchanged: only bond 1 changes, by −3%×40=−1.2, or −1.2% of the portfolio. KRD3=1.2.
  • 5-year rate up 1%: only bond 2 changes, by −5%×60=−3.0. KRD5=3.0.

Generally, for a portfolio of zero-coupon bonds, KRDi=wiDi, where wi is the weight of bond i and Di its modified duration.

  • The whole curve up 1% (a parallel shift): ΔP/P=−(1.2+3.0)×1%=−4.2%. The effective duration is ∑wiDi=4.2.

This is the key result: the sum of the key rate durations equals the effective duration,

EffDur=∑kKRDk

because a parallel shift is all the key rates moving together. It holds for any portfolio, not only zero-coupon bonds.

  • The curve steepens: the 3-year rate falls 1% and the 5-year rate rises 1%. In general,
ΔPP≈−∑kKRDk⋅Δrk

so here ΔP/P≈−[1.2×(−1%)+3.0×(+1%)]=−1.8%: the portfolio loses 1.8, even though its effective duration says nothing about a twist.

Any portfolio can be decomposed this way: each cash flow is a zero-coupon bond at its own date, so a coupon bond's key rate durations come from its cash flows near each key rate.

Managing Yield Curve ​

NOTE

Less important than KRD, but useful in practice.

In Level I, for a parallel shift: ΔPP≈−D⋅Δy+12C⋅(Δy)2.

With the three-factor decomposition above, Level II extends this to:

ΔPP≈−DLΔXL−DSΔXS−DCΔXC

The first term is the Level I parallel part; DS and DC are the sensitivities to steepness and curvature. All three are related to the KRDs, though not equal to any one of them.

Where DS and DC come from (mathematically). Let ℓk, σk and κk be the change in key rate k per unit of level, steepness and curvature. A factor move changes each key rate by

Δrk=ℓkΔXL+σkΔXS+κkΔXC

Substitute into the key rate formula and collect terms by factor:

ΔPP≈−∑kKRDkΔrk=−(∑kKRDkℓk)ΔXL−(∑kKRDkσk)ΔXS−(∑kKRDkκk)ΔXC

So each factor duration is the KRDs weighted by that factor's shape:

DL=∑kKRDkℓkDS=∑kKRDkσkDC=∑kKRDkκk

With ℓk=1 at every key rate, DL is just the sum of the KRDs, the effective duration. This is only the mathematics: neither the exam nor practice asks you to derive it. In practice the factor shapes are estimated statistically from past curve movements, and DS and DC are modeled as linear combinations of KRDs in exactly this way.

Example. A portfolio holds 1-year, 5-year and 10-year zero-coupon bonds, 100 in each position. With modified duration ≈ Macaulay duration = maturity, the weights are 1/3 each, so

KRD1=13,KRD5=53,KRD10=103

The factor shapes at the three key rates:

Year1510
Parallel (ℓk)+1 unit+1 unit+1 unit
Steepness (σk)−1 unit0+1 unit
Curvature (κk)+1 unit0+1 unit

Then DL, DS and DC follow by weighting the KRDs with each row:

DL=13+53+103=163=5.33DS=−13+0+103=93=3.00DC=13+0+103=113=3.67

Suppose the curve moves by ΔXL=+0.50%, ΔXS=+0.20% and ΔXC=−0.10%:

ΔPP≈−5.33×0.50%−3.00×0.20%−3.67×(−0.10%)=−2.90%

Check with the key rates directly. The move changes them by Δr1=0.50−0.20−0.10=+0.20%, Δr5=+0.50% and Δr10=0.50+0.20−0.10=+0.60%, so

ΔPP≈−(13×0.20%+53×0.50%+103×0.60%)=−2.90%

Interest Rate Volatilities ​

The term structure of interest rate volatility plots the volatility of yields against maturity. It is usually downward sloping: short-term yields are more volatile than long-term yields.

The difference in volatility can be explained by:

  • Short-term rates react to monetary policy, which changes frequently.
  • Long-term rates are linked to the real economy and long-run inflation expectations, which change more slowly.

Interest rate uncertainty is measured by the annualized standard deviation of the proportional change in a bond yield over a specified time interval. It matters most for bonds with embedded options, whose values depend directly on volatility.

NOTE

If changes in successive periods are uncorrelated (the usual model assumption), variance grows in proportion to time, so volatility scales with the square root of time:

σT=σannualT,σmonth=σannual112

For example, an annual volatility of 20% is a monthly volatility of 20%×1/12=5.77%.

Active Bond Portfolio Management ​

Forward Contract Strategy ​

NOTE

For the basic concepts of forwards, see Forward and Fixed-Income Forwards in Derivatives.

Recall the pure expectations theory: the forward rate is the market's estimate of the future spot rate, f(1,1)=E[s1(1)]. An investor whose own view differs from the forward rate can trade on it with a forward contract.

Take a forward contract, agreed at T=0, to buy at T=1 a one-year zero-coupon bond. Its forward price is set by the forward rate:

F0=1001+f(1,1)

At T=1 the bond is worth 100/(1+s1′), where s1′ is the one-year spot rate that actually prevails then:

  • s1′=f(1,1): the bond is worth exactly the forward price; the contract has no value.
  • s1′>f(1,1): the bond price is below the forward price, so the short gains and the long loses: Vshort>0, Vlong<0.
  • s1′<f(1,1): the bond price is above the forward price, so the long gains and the short loses: Vlong>0, Vshort<0.

So an investor who expects future rates to be lower than the forward rates imply goes long the forward (or buys longer bonds), and one who expects them to be higher goes short.

Example. With f(1,1)=2.80% (from the forward rate example), the forward price is F0=100/1.028=97.275.

  • If s1′=2.00%: the bond is worth 100/1.02=98.039, and the long gains 98.039−97.275=0.764.
  • If s1′=3.50%: the bond is worth 100/1.035=96.618, and the long loses 97.275−96.618=0.657.

Riding the Yield Curve ​

Riding the yield curve (rolling down the yield curve) means buying a bond with a maturity longer than the investment horizon and selling it at the horizon. It works when:

  • The yield curve is upward sloping, and
  • The yield curve is expected not to change over the horizon.

Then, as time passes, the bond "rolls down" to a shorter maturity with a lower yield, so its price rises. Buying a bond with a maturity longer than the investment horizon then gives a total return greater than a maturity-matching strategy.

Example. An upward-sloping curve, with prices of 3% annual-coupon bonds (par 100) of different maturities:

Maturity (years)YieldPrice
53.0%100.00
154.0%88.88
255.0%71.81
305.5%63.67

The investment horizon is 5 years. Ignoring the reinvestment of coupons:

  1. Maturity matching: buy the 5-year bond at 100 and hold it to maturity.
    • No capital gain or loss: the bond is redeemed at par.
    • Only credit and reinvestment risk.
    • Return: coupons of 5×3=15 on 100, so 15% over 5 years, about 2.8% a year.
  2. Riding the curve: buy the 30-year bond at 63.67 and sell it after 5 years. It is then a 25-year bond; if the curve is unchanged, its yield has rolled down from 5.5% to 5.0%.
    • Capital gain =71.81−63.67=8.14
    • Return: 71.81+15−63.6763.67=36.3% over 5 years, about 6.4% a year, more than the 30-year bond's own yield of 5.5%, because of the roll-down gain.

NOTE

The extra return is not free. The 30-year bond has far more interest rate risk: if the curve shifts up or flattens over the horizon, the roll-down gain shrinks or turns into a loss. The strategy is a bet that the curve will stay upward sloping and stable.

Developing Interest Rate Views Using Macroeconomics ​

NOTE

The details of this part are covered in Level III. For Level II, knowing the concepts is enough.

What moves yields.

  • Inflation (and inflation expectations) explains most of the variation in short- and intermediate-term government bond yields; the rest is attributable mainly to economic growth and monetary policy.
  • Monetary policy also moves long-term yields: through the expected path of future short rates, and through central bank purchases of bonds (quantitative easing), which lower long-term yields.

Bear and bull moves. A bear move means yields rise (bond prices fall); a bull move means yields fall. Flattening means the gap between long and short yields narrows; steepening means it widens.

  • Bearish flattening: short-term yields rise more than long-term yields. Typical when the central bank tightens monetary policy to cool down the economy.
  • Bullish steepening: short-term yields fall more than long-term yields. Typical during recessions, when the central bank cuts short-term rates to stimulate the economy.
Short-term yieldsLong-term yieldsTypical cause
Bear flatteningRise moreRise lessMonetary tightening
Bull steepeningFall moreFall lessMonetary easing in a recession
Bull flatteningFall lessFall moreFlight to quality
Bear steepeningRise lessRise moreFiscal deficits, inflation fears

Fiscal policy: supply-side effects. Yields tend to increase when budget deficits rise, because the government must issue more bonds. This is effectively a segmented market factor: the greater supply of long-term bonds increases the yield in that maturity segment.

Investor demand.

  • Domestic investor demand is a key driver: higher demand (e.g., from pension funds and insurers) raises bond prices and reduces the bond risk premium.
  • Non-domestic investor demand (e.g., foreign central banks and reserve managers) works the same way: external demand raises prices and reduces the bond risk premium.

Flight to quality. During highly uncertain market periods, investors flock to government bonds, in what is termed a flight to quality. It is often associated with bullish flattening: the curve flattens as long-term yields fall by more than short-term yields.

An investor who expects a bullish flattening may seek to profit from it by shifting from a bullet portfolio (concentrated in intermediate maturities) to a barbell portfolio (short and long maturities, with the same duration). The long end of the barbell gains the most when long-term yields fall, and the barbell's higher convexity adds to the gain.
